bullets: Factories and offices made fortunes for owners and businessmen like Scrooge (a moneylender and ‘man of business’).
Workers were paid low wages for long hours; there was little protection from unemployment, illness or injury.
Slums were overcrowded, dirty and dangerous. Stave 4’s description of the den where Old Joe trades stolen goods shows this underworld: foul streets, wretched houses.
Fog and smoke: Stave 1’s ‘fog came pouring in at every chink’ reflects polluted industrial London and symbolises moral blindness.
core.p: By 1843 Britain was the world’s leading industrial nation. London was the largest city in the world, growing fast as people moved from the countryside for work.

bullets: The **Children’s Employment Commission** (Second Report, 1843) described children working long hours in terrible conditions. Dickens was ‘perfectly stricken down’ by it.
Dickens himself worked in a blacking warehouse at 12.
In the novella: Martha Cratchit is an apprentice milliner working long hours; Peter is about to get a job; Tiny Tim is disabled and may die for lack of care.
**Ignorance and Want** (Stave 3) are ‘wretched, abject, frightful, hideous, miserable’ children who represent the products of neglect: lack of education and lack of food.

callouts.p: In 1843 Dickens visited the Field Lane Ragged School, which gave free education to destitute children. The Ghost’s warning that ‘Ignorance’ is the more dangerous child reflects Dickens’s belief that education was essential to prevent crime and social collapse.

core.p: Children worked in mines, factories, chimneys and workshops from a young age.

bullets: Tiny Tim is a symbol of the deserving poor child whose life depends on the generosity of the rich.
Ignorance and Want are a warning to society about the consequences of neglect: ‘Doom’.
Scrooge’s transformation into a ‘second father’ to Tiny Tim shows the role Dickens wanted the wealthy to play.

model: Cratchit children: poverty and family love
Tiny Tim: symbol of the deserving poor
Ignorance and Want: allegory and warning
Context: child labour, Commission report, Ragged Schools
exam.q: Explain how Dickens presents children elsewhere in the novella. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Children are central to Dickens’s purpose: always say why.

mistakes.r: He symbolises the poor child whose survival depends on society’s generosity.
mistakes.w: Tiny Tim is just a cute character.

quotes.a: Allegorical children: products of social neglect.
quotes.q: This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want.

quotes.a: Lack of education is the greatest danger.
quotes.q: most of all beware this boy

quotes.a: Starkly simple prediction about Tiny Tim.

summary: The Industrial Revolution created great wealth alongside crowded, dangerous slums, and child labour was widespread; the 1843 Children’s Employment Commission report shocked Dickens and directly inspired the novella’s focus on children such as Tiny Tim, Ignorance and Want.

terms.d: Characters representing abstract ideas (Ignorance and Want).
A free charitable school for destitute children.
